content: Chinese herbal medicines are widely used in China for the treatment of sore throat and are also utilized globally by practitioners of traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). However, their effectiveness in treating sore throat has not been systematically reviewed before. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Chinese herbal medicines in patients suffering from sore throat. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, AMED, the Chinese Biomedical Database (CBM), and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), covering studies published up to December 2011. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the use of Chinese herbal medicines for sore throat treatment. The outcomes measured were recovery rates, treatment inefficacy, and adverse events. Data extraction and analysis were performed by three review authors, with one author contacting the original study authors for additional information when necessary. A total of 12 studies involving 1,954 participants were included in the review. Among these, 10 studies were identified as being of poor methodological quality, while two studies were of medium quality. Due to the variability in study designs and outcomes, a meta-analysis was not performed; instead, the results were reported individually. Six specific Chinese herbal formulations demonstrated superior efficacy compared to their respective control treatments in improving recovery from sore throat: 1. Ertong Qingyan Jiere Koufuye was more effective than Fufang Shuanghua Koufuye for acute pharyngitis (odds ratio [OR] 2.52; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.11 to 5.74). 2. Yanhouling mixture outperformed gentamicin atomized inhalation for acute pharyngitis (OR 5.39; 95% CI 2.69 to 10.81). 3. Qinganlan Liyan Hanpian was more effective than Fufang Caoshanhu Hanpian for acute pharyngitis (OR 2.25; 95% CI 1.08 to 4.67). 4. Sore throat capsules were more effective than intravenous cefalexin (an antibiotic) for acute pharyngitis or acute tonsillitis (OR 2.36; 95% CI 1.01 to 5.51). 5. Compound dandelion soup was superior to sodium penicillin for acute purulent tonsillitis (OR 5.06; 95% CI 1.70 to 15.05). 6. A combination therapy involving eliminating heat by nourishing yin and relieving sore throat methods with Dikuiluqan Hanpian was more effective than Dikuiluqan Hanpian alone for children with chronic pharyngitis (OR 2.63; 95% CI 1.02 to 6.79). Additionally, six other Chinese herbal formulations were found to be equally effective as their control treatments. The authors concluded that while some Chinese herbal medicines appeared to be effective in treating sore throat based on the available evidence, the overall quality of the clinical trials was low. This raises concerns about the reliability of the findings. As a result, the efficacy of Chinese herbal medicines for sore throat remains uncertain, and no specific formulation can be recommended as a definitive treatment for sore throat at this time.
